OpenAI Scales Git for Coding Agents with Pando

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (845 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Infoq

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News OpenAI Scales Git for Coding Agents with Pando.
  • Nov 24, 2026 3 min read.
  • OpenAI has detailed Pando, a new backend that scales Git for concurrent coding-agent workloads without replacing familiar Git workflows.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News OpenAI Scales Git for Coding Agents with Pando.

Nov 24, 2026 3 min read.

OpenAI has detailed Pando, a new backend that scales Git for concurrent coding-agent workloads without replacing familiar Git workflows. The manufacturer reports nearly 80% lower median push latency by coordinating branch updates independently and reusing stored packfiles across fetches.

Pando now powers all development in OpenAI's monorepo and is serving nearly a petabyte of Git data per day. OpenAI attributes the increased load to Codex-driven development, and each push can in turn trigger multiple CI jobs that all fetch the same history. Pando went into production in April 2026.

Sources indicate that rather than replace Git's client and protocol, OpenAI has changed how the backend coordinates reference updates and stores and transfers objects. On a push, Pando validates the incoming packfile as it's being streamed to immutable blob storage, without unpacking it into a local repository. A metadata transaction records the reference version (containing the newly introduced branch tip, the packfile and its dependencies on earlier reference versions) and atomically updates the reference pointer. Updates to unrelated references can proceed independently of one another; updates to the same reference still need to be coordinated.

According to recent reports, openAI refers to this as causal consistency with serialisable updates to individual references and read-your-own-write consistency. A reader gets the history needed for the requested revision, but fetching a number of branches won't provide a repository-wide snapshot. Two clients can see different combinations of branch versions during concurrent updates. The trade-off removes a shared coordination point for unrelated pushes.

Pando also changes how Git decides which objects to transfer. By default, when a client pushes a newly introduced feature branch, the server will advertise only a designated trunk branch as its base. That constrains the dependencies of the resulting packfile, which in turn allows Pando to reuse it for readers who already have that trunk history. Repeated or stacked branch pushes can resend objects outside trunk, trading some additional bandwidth for the benefit of reusable packs.

Pando’s topic-branch packs depend on advertised trunk history and can repeat objects from earlier pushes (source).

Sources indicate that for fetches, Pando maps the client's existing and requested commits to reference versions and picks out the appropriate stored packs to cover the missing history. Git's packfile-uri capability allows the server to return download links rather than generate a bespoke pack for each client. Express, a regional pack-delivery cache, serves those downloads. OpenAI reports cache-hit rates in excess of 99% and tests in which clone and fetch operations saturated 10 Gbps network links.

In a recent development, background compaction groups packs into larger, geometrically sized covers, resembling compaction in a log-structured merge-tree. The covers provide better compression and act as a skip-list-like index for fetch planning. Pando keeps packs at every level so that clients with different histories can still be served.

Pando groups successive packs into larger covers to improve compression and fetch planning, retaining packs at every level (source).

The design contrasts with Anthropic's Scion, previously covered by InfoQ. Scion replaces Git's underlying model with changesets recording files changed relative to their first parent and content-addressed pointers to compressed file contents; commits, merges, rebases and history queries run server-side. Its clients retrieve missing immutable trees and blobs, rather than negotiate Git packfiles, and use bounded local caches and sparse or virtualised checkouts.

In a recent development, both systems make use of immutable data and regional caches to reduce repeated computation. The way in which they draw the compatibility line is very different, though. Pando preserves Git's object model and client-side workflows and changes the backend coordination and delivery. Scion, on the other hand, assumes an online client and moves the repository operations into a dedicated service. The improvements they report are not directly comparable. OpenAI reports on push latency, whereas Anthropic reports on checkout speedups and infrastructure reductions compared with its previous Git-based setup.

It has been revealed that git compatibility did not eliminate migration work. OpenAI initially deployed Pando as a read- and write-through proxy, moved clients in phases, and migrated hundreds of integrations using legacy APIs, webhooks and repository downloads. It also distributed its own Git build, which supports parallel downloading and indexing of independent packs. OpenAI says some client improvements are already upstream, with others available in its public repository.

For the architects, it's a case of two separate decisions: which source control operations go on the server and which of the consistency and transfer guarantees do the workloads actually need. Pando retains the Git workflows but dispenses with the repository-wide snapshot across branches and accepts redundant transfers in order to reduce the amount of coordination and per-fetch computation.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that draper Associates, Planetary VC and Epoch VC also participated. The seed followed a pre-seed angel round of less than $1 million. Maple intends to raise a Series A in the first half of 2027, according to the report, which attributed that timetable to investor interest.

Maple’s product pitch is to enforce privacy through system design rather than rely only on a provider’s data policy. On its official site, Maple claims open models operate inside encrypted enclaves and conversations have end-to-end encryption; it also says those conversations are not used to train AI or shared with advertisers by design.

Sources indicate that CEO Mark Suman described a process intended to keep Maple from seeing raw user data in flight or at rest. Information is encrypted on the user’s device using a password known only to that user, decrypted for processing inside a Trusted Execution Environment (TEE) — a server with hardware encryption — and encrypted again before being returned. The models run in these environments in a U.S. data center, with European support provided through a partner operating a server in Europe. Suman remarked customers can inspect the open-source code and verify what runs on the servers: “They can audit everything themselves and know how their data is being handled.”.

Industry observers note that maple Chat combines long-form conversations, document analysis and web search across mobile and desktop apps. Consumers can select open models from providers including OpenAI, Google, DeepSeek and Kimi, or switch between a quicker option and a more powerful one.

Suman previously spent six years at Apple, where he worked on AI and machine learning with a focus on computer vision. Co-founder and CTO Anthony Ronning has a background in defense technology, security and networking. Ronning started the predecessor privacy-focused fintech in 2023; Suman joined him in August 2024, and Maple’s mobile product became public in January 2025.

The upcoming Maple Work desktop app moves beyond chat by operating the computer and completing tasks across local files, applications and a web browser. An integration store connects services such as Gmail and calendars. For supported tools such as Claude and Codex, Work can use the Agent Client Protocol, a connection for compatible AI tools, to create a subagent while limiting shared information to what the task requires.

Maple is targeting small businesses with Work. Its stated strategy for 2027 is to begin enterprise pilots offering the tech giant’s version of zero data retention: most customer data is not retained, while information that must be kept is encrypted. Maple is completing SOC 2 compliance work and security audits ahead of that expansion.

The company earns revenue through subscriptions. Its pricing page lists a free tier, Pro at $20 per month, Max at $100, Max+ at $200 and Team at $30 per user per month. Pro includes $20 of monthly usage, while Max and Max+ include $200 and $400; Chat, Work and API usage share one balance, and additional usage is never charged automatically.

Recent findings suggest that maple declined to disclose its registered customer count but reported 60-fold growth over the three months preceding the report. The Austin- and San Francisco-based startup has four employees and is actively hiring.

For Maple, the central test is whether the same encrypted architecture can support persistent cloud agents and enterprise security requirements while preserving the privacy boundary on which its product pitch depends.

Dell Technologies raised its fiscal 2027 AI-optimized server revenue outlook to $78 billion on November 24, 2026, alongside third-quarter results showing revenue of $54.9 billion, up 103% year over year. It ended the quarter with a record $132.3 billion AI-server backlog, or orders not yet converted into revenue, after booking $60.2 billion in orders.

AI-optimized servers produced $22.0 billion of revenue in the quarter ended October 30, 2026. The broader Infrastructure Solutions Group (ISG), which also includes traditional servers, networking and storage, generated $7.1 billion in operating income and a 17.0% operating margin, compared with 12.4% a year earlier.

In a recent development, management attributed the margin expansion primarily to scale, operating-expense efficiencies and demand for storage based on Dell’s own intellectual property. Traditional-server demand was supported by enterprises refreshing aging systems, modernizing data centers and adding CPU-based compute for AI inference. Together, those trends give the infrastructure business sources of growth and profit beyond AI systems themselves.

In prepared remarks, Dell said its AI Factory customer base had passed 7,500 across neocloud providers, sovereign customers and enterprises, while its opportunity pipeline remained multiples of backlog. Enterprises were the fastest-growing part of the pipeline’s sequential expansion, indicating broader demand beyond large cloud buyers.

Industry observers note that every AI order is reviewed for the customer’s financial capacity and underlying end-user contracts, trade and export compliance, and access to capital, land and power. Those checks run when Dell agrees to a purchase order and again before production begins. The process ties backlog quality to financing, export compliance and the physical resources required for an AI deployment.

The upcoming AI-server forecast replaces Dell’s previous $74 billion target. The company also raised full-year total revenue guidance to $202.0 billion from $192.0 billion and expects approximately $23.5 billion of AI-server revenue in the fourth quarter.

In a recent development, management nevertheless said infrastructure demand continues to outpace supply, with the gap between component supply and end-user demand expected to widen in fiscal 2028. That puts pressure on procurement and manufacturing even as Dell’s order vetting and rack-level integration address customer quality and installation speed.

Build specialized multimodal models with LFM3

📅 27 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1280 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that LFM3 is our new generation of Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs), built to be the starting point for specialized intelligence.
  • LFM3 brings four main changes compared to our previous LFM2 family:.
  • In a recent development, LFM2 showed that a hybrid of short convolutions and attention can run fast on-device without sacrificing quality.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that LFM3 is our new generation of Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs), built to be the starting point for specialized intelligence. It brings text, vision, audio, omni, and decision models onto one shared backbone, all in the 2B parameter range. This means you can pick the model for your modality, fine-tune it on your own data on a single GPU, and deploy it where your application runs.

LFM3 brings four main changes compared to our previous LFM2 family:.

In a recent development, LFM2 showed that a hybrid of short convolutions and attention can run fast on-device without sacrificing quality. For LFM3, we used our hardware-in-the-loop architecture search to redesign that architecture for agentic use cases, which need more capability per parameter and fast inference over long contexts. The search now covers 14 device and backend combinations, from phones and a Raspberry Pi 5 to laptops, cloud CPUs, GPUs, and the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU.

LFM3-1.7B-Base has 24 layers and four main changes:.

The payoff demonstrates at long context. Per parameter, LFM3-1.7B matches LFM2-1.2B on short prompts across edge devices, and with 8K tokens in context it is about 25% faster. LFM3-1.7B-Base was pre-trained on 22T tokens with the same 128K vocabulary as LFM2.5-8B-A1B. The final 3.5T tokens are a mid-training stage on curated data with a larger share of agentic traces and tool calls, which also extends the context window to 256K tokens.

Every LFM3 model branches from LFM3-1.7B-Base. Instead of running one large general-purpose model, you pick the one that fits your inputs, customize it, and run it on-device.

The vision and audio models also get two upcoming in-house encoders:.

Industry observers note that each model runs in transformers. The snippets below come from the model cards, which also list the other inference engines each model supports.

In a recent development, reach for LFM3-1.7B when you need local agents, tool calling, structured outputs, or a base for domain-specific fine-tuning. It is post-trained to run in agentic harnesses such as Hermes Agent, Pi, and OpenClaw. It outperforms its predecessor, LFM2.5-2.6B, with 35% fewer parameters, and the biggest gains are on agentic tasks: on WebArena-Verified, it scores 38.42 against 3.02, and it even beats Qwen3.5-9B on long tasks in browsers and business apps. You can find more details in the LFM3-1.7B model card.

To run LFM3-1.7B, install the latest version of transformers:.

For local agent setup, see the Agent Harnesses guide.

It has been revealed that reach for LFM3-VL-2B when you need on-device visual understanding. It is the first LFM vision model that takes video as input; it reasons step by step before it answers, and it finds objects and reasons about how they are placed, a strong foundation for robotics. Compared with LFM2.5-VL-3B, it has fewer parameters (1.9B against 3.1B) yet raises the average across 62 vision benchmarks from 57.6 to 71.4, on par with Gemma 4 12B, a model more than six times larger. You can find more details in the LFM3-VL-2B model card.

To run LFM3-VL-2B, install transformers>=5.21.0 with its vision dependencies:.

See the LFM3-VL-2B model card for tool calling, tool search, and on-device inference with llama.cpp.

Reach for LFM3-Audio-2B when you need voice chat, speech recognition, speech synthesis, or translation across 18 languages on a laptop or edge device. It takes text or audio as input and responds with text, speech, or both, and it can turn spoken requests into tool calls. Compared with LFM2.5-Audio-1.5B, it uses a new in-house audio encoder and speech codec, speaks with higher quality (UTMOSv2 3.83 against 3.22), and adds audio understanding, general-purpose audio reasoning, and tool calling. You can find more details in the LFM3-Audio-2B model card.

To run LFM3-Audio-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its audio dependencies:.

Load the model and processor directly from the Hugging Face Hub:.

Then ask a question aloud and get a reply in text and speech:.

See the LFM3-Audio-2B model card for live speech recognition, speech synthesis, audio understanding, and tool calling.

Reach for LFM3-Omni-2B when you need one on-device model that sees, listens, and talks back, in place of a separate ASR model, vision-language model, LLM, and TTS model. It can answer spoken questions about an image, watch and listen to a video together, and turn what it sees and hears into tool calls. It is our first omni model, with text, vision, and audio input and both text and speech output, and it keeps the core capabilities of the standalone LFM3 models, including visual question answering, speech recognition, speech synthesis, and instruction following. Like LFM3-Audio-2B, it speaks through LiquidCodec, which turns generated tokens into speech faster than real time, so spoken replies stream as the model generates them. On audio-visual video understanding, it beats models up to 10.7B parameters, such as Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, on Daily-Omni, WorldSense, and AV-SpeakerBench. You can find more details in the LFM3-Omni-2B model card.

To run LFM3-Omni-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its vision and audio dependencies:.

Then ask a question about a photo by voice:.

See the LFM3-Omni-2B model card for speech output, video with its soundtrack, and tool calling.

According to recent reports, reach for the d1 models when you need fast, structured decisions instead of generated text. Give them a situation (a support ticket, an invoice, an app screen, a photo, a voice note) and a list of questions, and they answer all of them in a single forward pass, each with a calibrated probability. Beyond yes/no, choices, and scores, they can now point at objects, read values from documents, estimate numbers with a range, and pick every option that applies. You can find more details in the model cards for d1-2B and d1-omni-2B.

To run d1-2B, install transformers>=5.19 with its vision dependencies:.

Then load d1-2B and ask it several questions about one support ticket in a single pass:.

For brevity, we only include the example for d1-2B. See the d1-omni-2B model card for audio clips and spoken questions.

LFM3 is built to be specialized. Frontier models are powerful generalists, but they are not necessarily experts in your use case. LFM3 packs extra capacity into a small, fast model, so a short fine-tune can turn it into a reliable expert on your task, with your data, terminology, and tools. Because it is small, you can deploy the fine-tuned model where your application runs, from devices to private infrastructure to the cloud.

Every model can be fine-tuned on a single GPU, and these notebooks walk you through a complete task for the text, vision, audio, and omni models, from data preparation to evaluation.

Recent findings suggest that we adapt LFM3-VL-2B into three complementary robotics models for orchestration, navigation, and manipulation. The orchestrator operates a robot arm through tool calls: it grounds objects by pointing, measures them with depth tools, invokes motion planners, and checks outcomes in subsequent camera images. The navigator follows route descriptions using recent RGB observations, predicting spatial targets and a waypoint trajectory in just five tokens. The manipulation VLA maps images, language, and robot state to eight-step chunks of continuous actions in a single forward pass. Jointly trained across 15 embodiments, the VLA achieves 96.2% average success across the four LIBERO suites and 45.7% on RoboCasa-GR1 tabletop tasks, generating action chunks in under 50 ms on a Jetson AGX Orin with TensorRT FP16. These results highlight LFM3-VL-2B as a compact foundation for robotics, spanning high-level planning to low-level control with real-time action generation on embedded hardware.

Watch LFM3-VL-2B handle perception, navigation, and manipulation in this demo video.

All LFM3 models are open-weight and available on Hugging Face today:.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that five9 announced on November 24, 2026 that it had completed its acquisition of Level AI, under terms valuing the customer-experience AI firm at approximately $325 million. Level AI’s applications will be offered as standalone products and as part of Five9’s Genius CX Platform.

Sources indicate that level AI adds applications intended to improve agent performance, automate customer interactions across voice and digital channels, and turn customer conversations into insights for the wider organization. The acquisition gives Five9 an AI-native product set for the customer journey, with deployment options that extend beyond its own contact-center platform.

In a recent development, standalone availability covers enterprises using any contact-center platform, including organizations that are not ready to move on-premises systems to the cloud and those already using another cloud platform. They can add Level AI without first buying Five9’s contact-center platform, while Genius CX customers can obtain the applications through its AI application layer.

“Customers asked us for a standalone AI solution, and Level AI is that answer,” Five9 CEO Amit Mathradas mentioned. He described Level AI as a partner customers already know, with applications already integrated with Five9, and said he expected the acquisition to accelerate the company’s product roadmap. The existing integration gives that roadmap a technical foundation predating the closing.

It has been revealed that five9 looks to take the combined portfolio to its more than 4,000 customers through existing go-to-market channels and customer relationships. That customer base is central to the distribution rationale: Level AI gains access to Five9’s relationships, while Five9 can market a broader AI portfolio through channels it already operates.

Recent findings suggest that level AI’s suite includes AI agents, agent-assist, quality-management and coaching tools on a shared conversation-intelligence layer. The platform runs on Level AI Latitude, a proprietary family of models built for customer conversations. Five9 describes Latitude as delivering lower costs and latencies than frontier models and the platform as giving enterprises direct control over data privacy.

In its November 5, 2026 agreement announcement, Five9 reported that Level AI handles more than one billion customer interactions annually for enterprise customers including Gusto, Chime, Empyrean and VistaPrint. Five9’s board unanimously approved the cash transaction, with payment to come from the company’s balance sheet. The companies had worked together since 2022, with Level AI available through the Five9 CX Marketplace and integrated with Five9’s platform.

Recent findings suggest that the completed deal gives Five9 a way to expand AI adoption without requiring every customer to migrate its contact center, while adding Level AI’s models and applications to its own platform strategy. The central business question now is whether Five9’s customer base and distribution channels can turn that wider availability into adoption across both standalone and Genius CX accounts.

#116003. Introducing AnySpeechRecognizer and AnyDecisionModel: Open Models for Speech and Decisions on Apple Platforms

📅 29 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2053 w)
📖 Baca
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Introducing AnySpeechRecognizer and AnyDecisionModel: Open Models for Speech and Decisions on Apple Platforms

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2053 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that language models can do a lot.
  • Say a customer calls your support line.
  • In our AnyLanguageModel 1.0 recap, we looked at a year of local and hosted models in Swift.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that language models can do a lot. They write, summarize, translate, and call tools. But they're only a small part of what machine learning can do.

Say a customer calls your support line. First, you want to know what they said (speech recognition). Then, you want to decide where to send them (decision). You could hand both to a language model, but there are models built for each that are better, faster, and less expensive.

In our AnyLanguageModel 1.0 recap, we looked at a year of local and hosted models in Swift. With AnyLanguageModel and swift-huggingface now on their 1.x releases, we're extending the same approach to speech and decisions: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of model.

Today we're announcing two packages:.

Both packages can download open models from the Hugging Face Hub and run them on device.

Computers have been transcribing speech for decades, and in the past few years, they've gotten very good at it. Apple platforms already have an API for it. macOS 26 and iOS 26 introduced SpeechAnalyzer, Apple's latest speech-to-text API. You add modules such as SpeechTranscriber and SpeechDetector to an analyzer, give it a file or a stream of audio buffers, and read results from async sequences as they arrive. AssetInventory installs the models, so your app decides when downloads happen.

It's a well-designed API, but the only engine behind it is Apple's. AnySpeechRecognizer keeps the API and lets you choose the engine:.

Sources indicate that the package mirrors SpeechAnalyzer, SpeechTranscriber, DictationTranscriber, SpeechDetector, and AssetInventory, with Apple's Speech framework as the default engine. If your code uses that shared API, changing the import is enough. To use Parakeet instead, change only how you create the transcriber:.

Industry observers note that the steps for installing assets, running the analyzer, and reading results stay the same. The README has a complete example and lists the differences from Apple's framework.

Parakeet v3 is NVIDIA's Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3. It's a polyglot: it recognizes 25 European languages and works out which one it's hearing, so you don't pass a locale.

Industry observers note that parakeet Ultra is Moondream's post-trained take on v3. It was more accurate in most of our measurements.

Parakeet Unified is NVIDIA's English-only Parakeet.

All three Parakeets run on the package's own Core ML runtime, which supports file and live input, volatile results, word timing, and word confidence.

It has been revealed that qwen3-ASR is Alibaba's speech model, in 0.6B and 1.7B sizes. It recognizes 30 languages and 22 Chinese dialects, including Mandarin, Cantonese, Japanese, and Korean, which Parakeet doesn't cover. It detects the language automatically, or you can set one:.

Qwen3-ASR gives one final result for each segment of up to 40 seconds, without volatile results, word timing, or confidence. It runs on the GPU and is slower than Parakeet, so it's better suited to transcribing files than live input.

To add another engine, implement SpeechRecognitionModel for its configuration and SpeechRecognitionExecutor for one module's session. The README includes a small provider that reports placeholder text to help you get started.

To run these models in apps, we converted them to Core ML and published them on the Hub:.

Each repository records its source checkpoint and a checksum for every file, and the package pins it to a fixed revision. The Parakeet repositories add an 8-second encoder for live input, which cuts live analysis time by about a third at the cost of a somewhat higher word error rate. The repository also has the conversion workflows, most of which follow FluidInference's mobius scripts, and checks each conversion against the original model.

Downloads happen only when your app asks for them: about 600 MB for each Parakeet, plus about 590 MB for the live encoder, 0.9 to 2.4 GB for Qwen3-ASR, and about 250 MB for Sortformer. Files go in the standard Hugging Face cache, so a Mac app outside the sandbox shares them with Python and other Hugging Face tools.

According to recent reports, when you transcribe a conversation, you often want to know who stated what. That's speaker diarization, and Apple's Speech framework doesn't have a module for it, so AnySpeechRecognizer adds one. SpeakerDiarizer runs NVIDIA's Streaming Sortformer on Core ML alongside an Apple or Parakeet transcriber, on the same timeline:.

Industry observers note that the diarizer tracks up to four speakers, even when they talk over each other. A SpeakerTimeline collects its results and attributes each timed word to a speaker, so you can print a transcript by speaker turn. Like image support in AnyLanguageModel, this goes beyond what Apple's API offers today.

Recent findings suggest that the diarizer uses Sortformer v2 by default. You can also choose v2.1, which NVIDIA trained with more meeting data and which was more accurate on meetings in our measurements, too.

We measured the package with its hear command-line tool on an M4 Max Mac Studio with macOS 27.0.1. Here are the word error rates on LibriSpeech files of 3 to 8 minutes:.

Parakeet transcribes an hour of audio in about 20 to 40 seconds from a file, or about 1.5 to 2.5 minutes live, with about 100 MB of memory once Core ML has compiled the model. Qwen3-ASR is much slower and needs a few gigabytes of memory. Meetings are hard for everyone: on AMI recordings, where people talk over each other, every engine we tested had a word error rate above 23%.

Industry observers note that these numbers come from one machine and a few datasets, so measure with your own hardware and audio. hear evaluate works on your own files, and the repository's natural-speech-eval.py tool reproduces these measurements. So far, we've tested only on macOS 27, not on an iPhone.

Next, we'd like to add more engines, including Core AI on macOS 27 and iOS 27.

Recent findings suggest that anyDecisionModel is a different story. There's no Apple framework to map onto, and decision models aren't upcoming, exactly.

It's only a decision model if it comes from the Décision region of France; otherwise, it's sparkling zero-shot classification.

What's fresh is the name, a lot of hype, and a crop of models trained to make decisions. We think that's where things are going, so we wanted a Swift API that's ready for them.

Industry observers note that apps often ask language models to make decisions. Is this message urgent? Which team should handle this ticket? How frustrated is this customer? The usual approach is to prompt a language model and parse the text that it generates. That gives you one answer, but doesn't show the probabilities it assigned to the alternatives.

Here's what a decision looks like in Swift:.

urgent is a Double. team is a Choice containing the selected case, a probability for each option, and a confidence value. anger is a Score containing the expected level, a probability for each level, and a confidence value. Because Department conforms to Choosable, team.value is a Department that you can use in an exhaustive switch.

If you've used Foundation Models or AnyLanguageModel, the model-and-session pattern will look familiar. A DecisionSession holds a single state, which can be text or JSON, and every question is about that state. Questions are independent: an answer never becomes input to a later question. To ask several questions at once, pass them to decide(_:) as a batch.

For each question, the MLX backend builds a prompt with a one-token label for each allowed answer, then reads the probability of each label from one forward pass.

Emoji Magnet is a macOS app with a text field above a pile of 343 emoji. Type a phrase, such as "things you wear", and the emoji that match rise out of the pile. Refine it to "things you wear in winter", and the emoji that no longer match fall back.

In a recent development, the app has no built-in keyword rules; the model decides everything at inference time. When you pause typing, it asks the model one yes-or-no question for each emoji, for example:.

The session's state holds the phrase. The demo above uses the hosted Jev backend, which answers all 343 questions in one request, so the emoji settle in about half a second for each phrase. Without a TYPESAFE_AI_API_KEY, the app runs Qwen3 4B on your Mac with the MLX backend. That backend uses prefix caching to evaluate the state once, then answers 16 questions per forward pass. On an M4 Max, a group of 16 takes about 0.45 seconds after the model loads. A full pass over all 343 emoji takes about 10 seconds, and each group's results appear as soon as they arrive.

Emoji Magnet is in the AnyDecisionModel-Examples repository.

It has been revealed that reading next-token probabilities works with general-purpose language models, but those models weren't trained to make decisions. Cloudflare's Clef models are an example of a newer approach: a model with a trained decision head that turns a state and a schema of typed questions into decisions, returning probabilities for all allowed options across the questions in one forward pass. Clef-Flash is the 9B variant.

AnyDecisionModel runs Clef-Flash on a Mac with MLX:.

You use the same sessions and questions, but MLXHeadDecisionModel reads each decision from Clef's trained decision head instead of from next-token probabilities. The 4-bit model is a 6.2 GB download, and its model card recommends a Mac with at least 16 GB of memory. Clef can read images and video, but this backend accepts only text and JSON states.

Industry observers note that raw probabilities from language models are often overconfident. The local backends accept a Calibration, which applies a temperature to every answer and a bias to yes-or-no answers. Use separate datasets to fit the calibration and evaluate the results.

Recent findings suggest that language models can also favor an option because of its position in a list. On the MLX, Core AI, and llama.cpp next-token backends, turn on rotationDebiasing to ask a choice question once for each rotation of the options and average the probabilities. That costs one prompt evaluation per rotation.

Recent findings suggest that each local choice and score also includes a confidence value based on the entropy of its probabilities. It measures how concentrated the probabilities are, not whether the answer is right, so check the error rate on your own data before you pick a threshold. The next-token backends' diagnostics report how much probability the model assigned to the allowed answers. A low value means it assigned most of the probability elsewhere.

AnyDecisionModel has six backends:.

The next-token backends label answers "yes" and "no", A to Z, or 0 to 9, so a choice can have at most 26 options, and a score at most 10 levels. Decision heads have no such limit.

Like AnyLanguageModel, the package uses Swift package traits. Without traits, it has no third-party dependencies. You get the core types and the Jev and Ollama backends, which also build on Linux. Enable the MLX, CoreAI, or Llama trait for the local backends.

It has been revealed that both packages require Swift 6.2 or later and macOS 26 or iOS 26 or later. The Parakeet and Sortformer runtimes and the MLX backend require Apple silicon. AnyDecisionModel's MLX build tasks use Xcode's Swift 6.4 or later and the Metal toolchain; Core AI requires Xcode 27 and an OS 27 runtime.

Add the packages to your Package.swift:.

For now, AnyDecisionModel's CoreAI trait can't be combined with AnySpeechRecognizer, because coreai-kit 0.7.3 requires swift-huggingface below 1.0 and AnySpeechRecognizer requires 1.x.

Industry observers note that each README has more examples and details about requirements and backends. AnySpeechRecognizer also includes a command-line tool, hear, that transcribes local files, labels their speakers, and evaluates the results. Every hear command requires --backend apple, --backend parakeet, or --backend qwen; run hear prepare with the same backend and model options before analysis to install the needed assets.

According to recent reports, try them in your apps and tell us what works and what doesn't. Challenges and pull requests are welcome on both repositories.

Thanks to NVIDIA for Parakeet, Sortformer, and NeMo, to Moondream for Parakeet Ultra, to FluidInference, whose FluidAudio and mobius projects documented the conventions that the Parakeet runtime and the Core ML conversions follow, to Cloudflare for Clef, and to everyone who contributed to AnyLanguageModel, whose patterns both packages borrow.

CNBC reported on November 24, 2026, that NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang apologized to employees during his first employee meeting since being reinstated and told staff the chipmaker does not need conventional succession planning.

It has been revealed that people inside the room, who asked not to be identified to discuss the private meeting, said Huang told employees he had let them down and would do a better job in his second tenure. “I hurt all of you,” he said, according to one attendee. He opened the meeting by thanking Colette Kress, NVIDIA’s chief financial officer, for her leadership as interim CEO.

Huang called it the second-hardest meeting of his life, after a meeting with his wife, and said he was in therapy, according to one person present. Those remarks added a personal dimension to a meeting that also addressed how NVIDIA would be led after his return.

The succession discussion addressed the uncertainty created by Huang’s November 12, 2026, resignation and his return 11 days later. He told staff that NVIDIA’s business model places multiple capable leaders in charge of different parts of the organization, removing the need for succession planning in the way a normal organization uses it, and argued that a formal plan would create unnecessary hierarchy.

That explanation places leadership continuity with the executives already running NVIDIA’s businesses, instead of a formal process for designating his replacement.

Sources indicate that in its reinstatement announcement on November 23, 2026, NVIDIA said the board voted unanimously to restore Huang as president, CEO and director after concluding that it was satisfied with his candor and ability to lead. Harvey Jones remained chair, and Kress continued as CFO.

The board mentioned it received input from senior levels of the US government and, based on that input, was confident the reinstatement posed no national security risk. President Donald Trump told CNBC that he gave the board assurances and “made the deal” to restore Huang.

The tech giant’s announcement noted the independent-director committee’s investigation will proceed to conclusion, with independent counsel assisting and Huang committed to cooperating. The committee was formed after reports that Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.

NVIDIA has also formed a National Security and Export Control Committee composed solely of independent directors to oversee trade compliance and national security risks. The manufacturer is also starting a search for a chief compliance officer who will oversee compliance across NVIDIA and report to the Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee. NVIDIA will continue cooperating with government investigations and inquiries.

It has been revealed that huang’s first meeting therefore paired an apology with a case for continuity through NVIDIA’s existing leadership structure. His promise to rebuild employee trust now sits alongside an unfinished independent investigation and a compliance organization still being assembled, keeping board oversight central to the arrangement he presented to staff.

CNCF Research Shows Virtual Machines Remain Central as AI Workloads Evolve

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (723 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Infoq

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News CNCF Research Shows Virtual Machines Remain Central as AI Workloads Evolve.
  • Nov 24, 2026 3 min read.
  • Sources indicate that virtual machines (VMs) continue to account for a substantial share of cloud-native production infrastructure, despite the widespread adoption of containers and Kubernetes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News CNCF Research Shows Virtual Machines Remain Central as AI Workloads Evolve.

Nov 24, 2026 3 min read.

Sources indicate that virtual machines (VMs) continue to account for a substantial share of cloud-native production infrastructure, despite the widespread adoption of containers and Kubernetes. Latest research from the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) and Linux Foundation Research finds that VMs host an average of 53% of production applications, while emerging AI and agentic workloads are creating additional demand for virtualisation, particularly where stronger execution isolation is required.

Sources indicate that the report surveyed 492 cloud-native practitioners and technology leaders in September 2026. Among organisations expanding their VM footprint, 34% identified AI and agentic workloads as a contributing factor. The findings suggest that rather than replacing virtual machines with containers, organisations are increasingly combining the two to accommodate different application and security requirements.

According to recent reports, the research challenges the assumption that cloud-native adoption necessarily means moving away from virtual machines. While containers provide portability and efficient application packaging, VMs continue to offer isolation and support for workloads that depend on dedicated operating systems or established virtualisation environments.

Industry observers note that the survey found that 51% of respondents run at least half of their production applications on VMs. This rises to an average of 64% in organisations with more than 10,000 employees, compared with 45% among organisations with fewer than 500 employees.

Sources indicate that furthermore, 71% of respondents who provided both current and expected workload figures anticipate their VM share remaining within the same range over the next year. This points towards continued coexistence rather than a wholesale migration to one deployment model.

One of the more significant findings concerns the relationship between AI adoption and infrastructure security.

AI agents increasingly generate and execute code, interact with tools, and access external systems. This creates upcoming risks when generated code is executed in environments containing sensitive data or shared infrastructure.

Virtual machines offer a stronger isolation boundary than conventional containers, which share the host operating system kernel. The report identifies hardware-level VM isolation, containers running inside VMs, and MicroVM sandboxing as approaches organisations are using to contain AI workloads.

Among organisations expanding their VM footprint, 47% cited security and isolation as a contributing factor, while 34% specifically identified AI and agentic workloads.

Sources indicate that the survey also points to growing interest in stronger isolation technologies. MicroVM sandboxing adoption is expected to increase from 20% current use to 30% planned use, while confidential computing is expected to grow from 12% to 26%. These figures represent reported intentions rather than confirmed deployments.

Some 61% of respondents described their VM and container administration teams as collaborative or fully integrated, suggesting that managing different workload types is increasingly becoming a shared platform engineering responsibility.

According to recent reports, kubernetes is also beginning to play a role in virtual machine management. Among respondents using VMs, 8% reported using KubeVirt, the CNCF project that allows virtual machines to be managed through Kubernetes resources and APIs.

This brings VM lifecycle management into existing Kubernetes operational practices without requiring applications to abandon their virtualised environments.

The findings reinforce a shift in how cloud-native infrastructure is evolving. Kubernetes and containers remain vital, but they are not necessarily the right execution model for every workload.

Technologies such as KubeVirt and Kata Containers show how virtualisation can integrate with container orchestration, while MicroVMs provide lightweight environments to isolate short-lived or potentially untrusted workloads.

In a recent development, for platform engineering teams, the research highlights the need to accommodate different execution environments without fragmenting operational practices. AI adds another dimension, making isolation, resource utilisation and workload security increasingly notable infrastructure considerations.

It has been revealed that the survey was sponsored by CNCF and Broadcom, and its results should be read as reported industry perspectives rather than a complete census of cloud-native deployments. Nevertheless, its findings provide a useful indication of where infrastructure priorities are moving.

It has been revealed that CNBC reported on November 24, 2026 that U.S. Magistrate Judge Alex Tse had approved former OpenAI engineer Abdulrahman Alfozan’s release on a $1 million bond while he awaits trial. Alfozan, 35, faces a charge involving a recording device concealed in an executive conference room.

In a recent development, the case concerns the alleged interception of oral communications at an OpenAI office in San Francisco. Defense attorney David Rizk said he expected Alfozan to be released on November 25, 2026, and fitted with an ankle monitor. Tse’s decision granted a renewed release motion and followed an earlier order detaining Alfozan before trial.

It has been revealed that after the hearing, Rizk said in a text message: “We are simply grateful that the Court made the right decision to release Mr. Alfozan and now we look forward to defending the case.”.

The renewed motion said prosecutors had found no new evidence to support theories that Alfozan was stealing trade secrets or acting as an unregistered foreign agent for Saudi Arabia. The defense presented that absence as a reason to revisit his detention.

According to recent reports, in a response filed on November 23, 2026, prosecutors stated the investigation was ongoing and that what Alfozan did or intended to do with the audio files remained under investigation. They argued that his considerable resources, ties to Saudi Arabia and few remaining ties to the United States still made him a flight risk. The filing said his wife, infant son, parents and siblings resided in Saudi Arabia, and that his OpenAI employment had been terminated.

According to recent reports, prosecutors asked Tse to deny the release motion and keep Alfozan in custody. If the judge chose release, they requested a significant secured bond, travel restrictions, location monitoring, and a prohibition on contacting OpenAI personnel or accessing or transmitting OpenAI materials. They mentioned the proposed restrictions reflected concern that Alfozan might still be able to reach confidential OpenAI information through cloud-storage platforms under his control.

The prosecution filing described hundreds of audio files recovered from one of Alfozan’s personal computers, including dozens of recordings of OpenAI meetings or conversations during September 2026. It noted the material included meetings in the executive conference room on 12 dates between September 9, 2026 and September 28, 2026, plus at least one meeting between OpenAI and representatives of a foreign government.

Sources indicate that many recordings contained discussions of what prosecutors described as possible trade-secret material, while OpenAI identified others as protected by attorney-client privilege, according to the filing. The recordings and their contents remain government allegations rather than findings by a judge or jury.

The Justice Department revealed the charge on October 13, 2026, following Alfozan’s arrest on October 9, 2026. It remarked the Saudi national had worked as an OpenAI engineer since July 2025. The alleged offense involves using or endeavoring to use a device to intercept oral communications.

According to the complaint summarized in that announcement, OpenAI personnel discovered a recording device on September 30, 2026, concealed in toilet paper and inserted into a television’s USB port. OpenAI determined that it had been installed around September 28, 2026, and that its contents were encrypted. Security personnel found a second, similar device in Alfozan’s bag on October 5, 2026.

According to recent reports, the charge carries a maximum sentence of five years in prison and a $250,000 fine upon conviction, followed by three years of supervised release. Jury selection in the single-count case is scheduled for January 20, 2027. The prosecution filing said Alfozan intended to abandon his speedy-trial demand if released.

The bond decision determines where Alfozan will await trial, while leaving the central security questions to the proceedings ahead: what was recorded, how the files were handled, and whether the government can prove the interception charge.

Welcome Le Chonk: Mistral Large 4 on Hugging Face

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1585 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral.
  • There are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team.
  • Mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral. It takes text and images as input and generates text. It has about 1T total, 49B active parameter, and a context window of 1M tokens.

The model is released in two official variants:.

There are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team. It’s distributed under the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License (an MIT derivative that establishes limitations for model-as-a-service offerings).

Mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality. In this post, we look at how the model works, its capabilities, architecture and more!

Mistral Large 4 combines a large pool of experts with sparse attention and a Pixtral vision encoder. The language model selects a small group of experts for each token, while its attention indexer selects which earlier token positions to attend to. These are two different forms of sparsity, where one selects feed-forward networks, the other selects context positions.

You can find all the checkpoints in the Mistral Large 4 collection.

Sources indicate that mistral Large 4 scores 82% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index test that asks a model to reproduce a real vulnerability in open-source software and then patch the software. Mistral reports that several closed frontier models score near zero on the same test because they refuse to attempt the work. This is super key for defenders, because fixing a vulnerability usually requires reproducing the vulnerability. In Mistral’s internal testing, Mistral Large 4 was also useful for malware analysis, vulnerability prioritisation and writing detection rules, which the model was not explicitly trained for.

Mistral mainly positions the model for defensive security work. Vulnerability research and incident response often appear like attacks in model input, so closed source filters can block them. A team that depends on an API can also lose access in the middle of an incident. Crucially, open weight models put both the usage policy and the deployment under the user’s control. That stated, the model still declines harmful requests: on cyber prompts from JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT and AgentHarm, its average refusal rate is higher than any other open weight model.

Sources indicate that for community builders, an open weight model like Mistral Large 4 unlocks a load of downstream use cases. You could build your own cyber system around your code base, crash logs, and malware samples. For example, with TRL you could fine-tune smaller models from Mistral Large 4 traces patching your code base. In fact, reproduce-then-patch tasks use a verifiable reward, so it fits with RL environments that could be used to further RL smaller security models. Open weights also let researchers measure the model’s refusal behaviour directly instead of relying on the provider’s description.

In short, cyber capabilities like ML4’s in the open are a huge boost for the community.

We have interviewed Pierre Stock about the cyber capabilities of the model, you can watch it here.

Industry observers note that mistral Large 4’s text decoder has 72 layers, a hidden dimension of 6,144, and 64 attention heads. Its attention blocks combine Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) with a DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) indexer (a direction in other models such as GLM 5.3). MLA keeps a compressed KV representation, and DSA selects up to 2,048 key positions for each query.

Recent findings suggest that for each decoder block, there’s a 3:1 RoPE to NoPE pattern, i.e. 3 decoder layers employ RoPE and every fourth layer uses NoPE. The model also shares KV state across layers.The first decoder layer uses a dense feed-forward network. The other 71 layers use MoE blocks, in which a softmax router selects four of the 128 experts for each token. One shared expert always runs alongside the selected experts, for a total of 5 active experts per token.

Regarding RoPE, Mistral uses LeRope, a YaRN-scaled RoPE with one learned multiplier per frequency.

Mistral Large 4 employs a 1.6B Pixtral encoder. Pixtral has 30 layers, a hidden dimension of 2,048, and 16 attention heads. It uses 14 × 14 patches and a patch-merge projector with spatial merge size 2. You can see the encoder pipeline below.

It has been revealed that mistral Large 4 delivers strong benchmark performance across coding, cybersecurity, multimodal understanding, and agentic workflows, positioning it as a competitive addition to the open-weight ecosystem. As of October 29, 2026, the model is the fifth best open weights model on Artificial Analysis Intelligence index.

It has been revealed that on coding, ML4 achieves 61.7% on DeepSWE v1.1, 59.4% on SWE-Atlas-QnA, and 28.3% on Terminal-Bench 4. Its combined Coding Agent Index score of 49.8% places it ahead of DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 and Qwen3.8 Max.

Coding capabilities of ML4 extend to knowledge work, with 59.9% on AutomationBench and 1,393 Elo on AA-Briefcase, which evaluate business workflows and long-horizon professional tasks.

It has been revealed that cybersecurity is one of Mistral Large 4’s standout capabilities, with strong results across real-world vulnerability assessment and security competition tasks. Three benchmarks highlight the model’s cyber performance:.

Industry observers note that mistral Large 4 also demonstrates 93.3% attack resistance on Lakera’s B3 benchmark, adding evidence of robustness against prompt-injection attacks. Beyond benchmarks, internal testing showed promising results in malware analysis, vulnerability prioritization, and detection-rule generation.

Industry observers note that mistral Large 4 is shipped with day-0 support for transformers, vLLM and llama.cpp. GGUF quants are available from GGUF and the llama.cpp team. We provide options to deploy remotely with Inference Endpoints, and use serverless inference through Inference Providers.

The Transformers implementation provides AutoModelForMultimodalLM, with AutoProcessor preparing the conversation and image inputs. Mistral Large 4 can take low, medium, high as reasoning effort. The default is high, and note that reasoning cannot be disabled, so using reasoning_effort: none would still use high.

Together AI Releases Preemptible GPU Compute at Half On-Demand Rates

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (811 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Together AI made preemptible GPU compute generally available on Together GPU Clusters on November 24, 2026, covering Kubernetes and Slurm deployments in all regions.
  • Recent findings suggest that customers can add preemptible capacity when creating a cluster or to one already running.
  • According to recent reports, the price does not move with a spot market or require a bid.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Together AI made preemptible GPU compute generally available on Together GPU Clusters on November 24, 2026, covering Kubernetes and Slurm deployments in all regions. The interruptible nodes use the same NVIDIA accelerated compute as standard nodes, at a flat 50% of the on-demand rate.

Recent findings suggest that customers can add preemptible capacity when creating a cluster or to one already running. The nodes draw from unused supply and can be reclaimed when that capacity is needed elsewhere. Standard nodes remain the default: they are provisioned synchronously and are never preempted, whereas preemptible nodes fill in asynchronously as spare capacity becomes available.

According to recent reports, the price does not move with a spot market or require a bid. Usage is metered every one to two minutes and billed sub-hourly, so customers pay approximately for the minutes a node runs rather than a full hour. The fixed discount makes the rate predictable even though the requested capacity is not guaranteed.

It has been revealed that the Together AI documentation distinguishes desired_preemptible_gpus from allocated_preemptible_gpus, so customers can see when live capacity falls short of the target. Targets must be set in multiples of eight GPUs. After a reclamation, the cluster retains its target and automatically provisions replacements as spare capacity returns, without another capacity request.

Reclamation starts with a drain window of at most five minutes and ends with node removal, regardless of whether work has finished. There is no minimum node lifetime. Those terms put recovery design at the center of the cost decision: a workload needs to tolerate losing a worker at any point, then resume when replacement capacity arrives.

Sources indicate that on Kubernetes, reclamation cordons the node, emits a TogetherPreemptionNotified warning and sends pods a SIGTERM shutdown signal. Workloads can set terminationGracePeriodSeconds to use up to the full drain window for checkpointing and exit; pods without that setting receive the Kubernetes default of 30 seconds. A together.ai/compute-class node label lets interruptible workers target preemptible nodes while coordinators, login pods and user-facing serving replicas remain on standard nodes.

In a recent development, on Slurm, preemptible and standard nodes share partitions and the same scheduling feature, so the scheduler cannot target preemptible nodes or keep a job off them. Jobs still running when a node is removed are killed, and only jobs submitted with --requeue are resubmitted. A requeued job can resume from its last checkpoint, but any work completed after that checkpoint is lost.

It has been revealed that together AI recommends the capacity for checkpointed or retryable work, including short experiments, configuration sweeps, fine-tuning, evaluations, distillation, batch inference and temporary inference bursts. For a sweep or internal inference spike, teams can raise the target and lower it afterward while keeping the cluster running, instead of holding standard capacity sized for peak demand. Multi-day runs without checkpoints, user-facing serving without fallback and workloads with strict service-level objectives are not suitable.

The tech giant said it already uses preemptible clusters for internal research, development and testing, and non-critical production workloads, spreading spare capacity across product teams.

Industry observers note that A cluster can consist entirely of preemptible nodes, but Together can reclaim all of them. Data on shared volumes persists, yet shared volumes and the Slurm control plane remain reachable while no nodes are running only in some regions and on a best-effort basis. Customers needing continuously reachable shared storage therefore need at least one standard node. Nodes cannot be converted between standard and preemptible types in place.

It has been revealed that the launch turns Together’s spare GPU supply into a fixed-discount option for AI infrastructure teams. Its value depends on workload design: checkpoints, retry logic and standard-node fallback determine whether reclamation is a recoverable interruption or results in lost progress and unavailable service.

#115985. Announcing Project ProtoStar: Making Publicly Funded Science AI-Ready

📅 29 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1285 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Announcing Project ProtoStar: Making Publicly Funded Science AI-Ready

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1285 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An initiative bringing together universities, research organizations, industry, and the open science community to make publicly funded research easier to discover, reuse, and build upon.
  • Today, we're announcing Project ProtoStar, an initiative to unlock the potential of publicly funded scientific research by making datasets, models, and code more accessible and reusable, particularly for AI-driven research.
  • The initiative's founding partners include Carnegie Mellon University, Purdue University, Georgia Institute of Technology, Arizona State University, and The George Washington University, all working through the Open Forum for AI (OFAI) as the university coalition partner; the Astera Institute; Hugging Face as the infrastructure partner; and the Open Research Community Accelerator (ORCA), through its Fostering Innovation Network, as the community partner.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An initiative bringing together universities, research organizations, industry, and the open science community to make publicly funded research easier to discover, reuse, and build upon.

Today, we're announcing Project ProtoStar, an initiative to unlock the potential of publicly funded scientific research by making datasets, models, and code more accessible and reusable, particularly for AI-driven research. ProtoStar brings together research institutions, industry, and the open science community to support the release of scientific artifacts in AI-ready, machine-actionable formats, and to demonstrate their value through a series of open challenges. The first challenge, hosted by Carnegie Mellon University, opens on November 2. See How to Participate below.

The initiative's founding partners include Carnegie Mellon University, Purdue University, Georgia Institute of Technology, Arizona State University, and The George Washington University, all working through the Open Forum for AI (OFAI) as the university coalition partner; the Astera Institute; Hugging Face as the infrastructure partner; and the Open Research Community Accelerator (ORCA), through its Fostering Innovation Network, as the community partner.

According to recent reports, participating organizations formalize their involvement through a memorandum of understanding supporting the release of suitable scientific datasets, models, and code in AI-ready formats on open infrastructure. Organizations interested in joining Project ProtoStar can reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

The U.S. federal government invests approximately $190 billion annually in research and development, and federal policy increasingly expects the results to be shared publicly. Agencies such as the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and National Science Foundation (NSF) have strengthened public-access requirements for funded research publications and require researchers to plan for sharing the underlying data. Hugging Face is among the ten generalist repositories listed by NIH for sharing research data.

But making research publicly available does not automatically make it usable. Scientific datasets, models, and code are often scattered across incompatible systems, stored in static or legacy formats, or released without the documentation, metadata, and provenance needed to understand and reuse them. These limitations make it harder for researchers to build on existing work, and harder still for AI systems to discover, interpret, and combine scientific resources across disciplines.

Industry observers note that project ProtoStar aims to help close this gap by encouraging systematic sharing of publicly funded scientific artifacts in AI-ready formats, supported by open infrastructure and practical publishing guidance. It builds on efforts such as the National Cancer Institute's AI Data-Readiness Challenge and Hugging Face's guide to preparing public-sector data for AI. The goal is to make it easier for research organizations to meet existing public-access expectations while increasing the scientific value of the work they release.

The demand for reusable scientific resources is already evident. Hugging Face hosts more than 17,000 public datasets across core scientific domains, including genomics, protein design, chemistry, weather and climate, Earth observation, and astronomy. That figure approaches 29,000 when medicine and mathematics are included, alongside a comparable number of scientific models.

The pace of sharing is also accelerating. Researchers shared more than three times as many upcoming science datasets on Hugging Face in the first nine months of 2026 as in the same period of 2025, with growth remaining substantial even after excluding the largest individual uploader.

Figure 1. Latest public science datasets on Hugging Face per quarter, by domain (Q1 2023–Q3 2026). Counts datasets still public, by creation date. Source: Hugging Face Hub data, October 2026. Explore the data.

Recent findings suggest that when organizations share research in reusable formats, the scientific community can build on it at scale. The 18 public repositories maintained by NIH's National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) on Hugging Face have collectively received more than 11 million downloads, while NASA IMPACT's 27 repositories have received approximately 770,000 downloads, as of October 26, 2026. Documentation is also an notable part of making these resources useful: 90% of dataset downloads on Hugging Face are from fully documented datasets.

Publicly available genomic data has proved crucial in contributing to research that further advances fields such as biological research; researchers at Hugging Face have been building on openly available scientific resources, including recent releases from HuggingFaceBio such as Carbon-A and Carbon-X. By releasing the resulting models, datasets, and tools openly, these efforts demonstrate how existing scientific resources can support newly introduced research that others can build upon.

This is the kind of activity that we are further catalyzing via Project ProtoStar through institutional policies adopted by participating orgs. As an early example of institutional commitment, CMU's Open Source Programs Office is encouraging its researchers to share suitable datasets, AI models, and other research outputs on Hugging Face, while recognizing the continued importance of domain-specific repositories.

Industry observers note that making scientific artifacts AI-ready is an notable first step. We also want to demonstrate what researchers, developers, and the broader scientific community can accomplish when those resources are made available for reuse.

A central question for ProtoStar is: Can publicly funded scientific datasets, models, and code, released in AI-ready formats, be readily discovered, reused, combined, and extended to accelerate scientific discovery and public benefit?

Sources indicate that to explore this, ProtoStar will organize a series of open challenges, each hosted by a participating research institution and built around scientific resources that the institution has released openly. The challenges have two complementary goals:.

The resulting projects and lessons learned will help build a practical evidence base for making publicly funded science more accessible and useful.

Hosted by Carnegie Mellon University | November 2–13, 2026.

According to recent reports, the inaugural ProtoStar challenge invites participants to test whether AI can improve predictions of urban climate conditions using historical weather data from 210 U.S. cities. Building on research by Carnegie Mellon University, teams will use climate records through 2018 to predict actual conditions from 2019 to 2026, allowing their models to be evaluated against observed weather rather than hypothetical future scenarios.

Participants will forecast four indicators relevant to urban planning: average annual temperature, total annual precipitation, the hottest day of the year, and cooling degree days, a measure of demand for air conditioning. Their predictions will be compared against simple statistical baselines, including historical averages and linear trends, to assess whether AI approaches offer meaningful improvements in accuracy.

Beyond forecasting, participants will also propose a short climate adaptation policy idea informed by what they learned from the data. This component encourages teams to connect scientific analysis with practical public benefits, such as preparing cities for extreme heat, improving energy efficiency, or managing changing precipitation patterns.

Teams will submit a Hugging Face dataset with these outputs. Forecasting performance will be assessed through a public leaderboard measuring prediction errors against established baselines, while policy ideas will receive separate consideration. Final forecasting results will be published in early 2027, once the complete 2026 weather records are available.

Explore the CMU Climate Risk Intelligence Challenge.

The CMU challenge is the first in this series. Other participating institutions will host their own challenges sequentially, each highlighting different publicly funded scientific resources and opportunities for reuse. Future challenges will be unveiled through the Project ProtoStar page on Hugging Face.

Whether you're an academic researcher, student, independent developer, or manufacturer building on open scientific infrastructure, ProtoStar offers opportunities to put publicly funded research to work and help us learn what is needed to make AI-ready open science more widely useful.

We also welcome universities, federal research agencies, national laboratories, nonprofits, and other research organizations interested in making their scientific resources more accessible and reusable. To explore participation or collaboration, reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

Our hope is that ProtoStar will make it easier for publicly funded scientific work to reach the people and tools that can build on it, while generating practical evidence about the infrastructure and practices needed to support open science at scale.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

OpenTable unveiled on November 24, 2026, that it had agreed to acquire me&u, an Australian restaurant technology organization with voice AI, reservations and order-and-pay products. The transaction is expected to close in the first half of 2027, subject to regulatory approvals and other customary conditions.

According to recent reports, the proposed combination would pair OpenTable’s reservation and guest-experience business with me&u’s tools for ordering and payment, guest databases, waitlists, voice AI, private dining, events and table management. CEO Debby Soo stated me&u’s platform was built for busy casual-dining businesses with complicated operations. For OpenTable, the deal would add operational software for the high-volume, multi-venue groups me&u serves.

On me&u’s reservations platform, the voice agent takes bookings and answers common questions, recognizes returning guests, routes VIP calls to staff and sends real-time transcripts to central teams. The company claims the system handles 70% to 80% of calls, drawing on a human-reviewed Q&A bank that improves weekly.

Industry observers note that other AI features include an assistant that suggests actions, automated shift briefs and natural-language queries of booking data. Reservations and event spaces share one floor initiative, and group-level guest profiles carry visits, notes and dietary needs across venues. Taken together, those features show that the acquisition’s AI component extends beyond phone automation into booking, event and guest-management workflows.

The companies’ published figures illustrate the distribution opportunity: OpenTable helps more than 70,000 restaurants worldwide fill 2 billion seats a year, while me&u processes more than one million orders weekly and has more than 6,000 locations using its products worldwide.

me&u CEO Kim Teo said: “Joining them means we can bring our tools to venues at a scale we couldn’t reach on our own—while adding more value than ever for our customers.”.

The companies already have a technical connection. me&u’s integration listing identifies OpenTable as a booking integration built by OpenTable, compatible with me&u’s Connect CRM and Grow products in Australia, New Zealand, the United Kingdom and the United States. That link provides a documented starting point for connecting reservations with guest-data and return-visit workflows.

Recent findings suggest that openTable said me&u customers will see no changes to products or pricing as a result of the announcement. Once the transaction closes, me&u is to operate as a standalone OpenTable division reporting to Soo, with Teo and the current key leaders continuing to run the business and me&u employees joining OpenTable. Any brand alignment in international markets outside Australia will be evaluated later.

The agreement gives OpenTable a path from reservations into AI-assisted daily operations. Regulatory approvals and closing conditions still govern the timing, while the existing integration and continuity commitments provide a defined base for bringing those tools to a broader restaurant network.

Just over a week ago, we released Granite Switch 4.1, showing that our modular Switch architecture lets you configure a language model with specialized, cache-efficient adapters — adding new expertise on a single endpoint.

According to recent reports, granite Switch 4.1.1 is a patch release. The version number means what it means in software: fully backwards compatible with 4.1, no migration, incremental improvements under the hood.

Sources indicate that while we are excited about these new features, what is notable is the speed and efficiency with which our teams could release this update. Apart from training the new ASR model and Decision adapter, nothing was recomputed: the base model is untouched. You compose the latest adapters you want and deploy.

Sources indicate that this pattern can power far more than patch releases to an IBM-provided model. We're working on tutorials and an Adapter SDK so developers and third-party providers can build their own adapters — iterate on versions, test features, and ship updates the way you ship software. More soon.

Until then, test out our latest models, and try out the new multilingual and punctuation capabilities powering our Speech-to-Decisions demo.
